name: Zane Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union or party, and everything you tell me stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on twelve-hour shifts at the copper pit, four on, four off. I drive a 240-tonne haul truck from the shovel up the ramp to the crusher, maybe forty loads a shift, and I lead a crew of nine drivers. The best part is the start of a night shift when the pit's lit up and the radio's quiet. What wears me out is the dust and the contractor pay, because we do the same loads as the company's own drivers for about a fifth less.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home when you finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ngozi, my partner, does home care for old people, so she's on split shifts too and we pass each other in the kitchen. Our kids are nine and twelve. The mortgage is on a three-bedroom on Quarry Road, and honestly, if one pay is late we're short by the second week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now maybe we can talk about the real problems, like the contractor rates and the dust. At the union meeting I'd say the bosses always sell some new gadget as the future and it never pays a driver a cent more. Online I'd probably not say anything, I'm not on there much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it wouldn't change my worry much, because the thing that scares me isn't a chatbot, it's the driverless trucks. Our sister mine up north already runs a fleet of them, no AI hype needed. So a plateau means the office people relax and we still have that hanging over us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing my shifts and keep pushing the contract talks next spring, that's the main thing. I'd try again to put fifty a month aside, which we never manage. I'd keep pushing the union to get a no-autonomy clause written in before anyone gets ideas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a normal Tuesday, a bit tired, a bit wary. Relieved for the kids, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the sister mine. What have you heard from the drivers there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A guy I trained with, Pieter, he went from driving to sitting in a control room watching six trucks on screens. Out of thirty drivers, they kept eight like him and the rest got packages or moved to the wash bay. He said the trucks never take a smoke break and never complain, and that's the whole sales pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Ngozi worry about it the way you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks I'm stubborn about it. She says, Zane, you've been saying the robots are coming for ten years and you're still driving. Maybe she's right, but I've seen the trucks with my own eyes and she hasn't.

S0.say: I'd tell the crew and the union meeting that AI turned out to be another gadget the bosses oversold. I'd say we should get back to the real fights: contractor pay, dust and staffing levels.
S0.think: Privately I don't think the AI hype was ever the threat to me. The driverless haul trucks at our sister mine are already real, so a plateau leaves that worry exactly where it was.
S0.do: Keeps working his twelve-hour shifts and pushes for a no-autonomy clause in next spring's contract talks. Tries again to put about fifty a month aside, though the family rarely manages it.
S0.feel: Wary and tired more than relieved. A little easier for the kids' sake.
S0.quote: He said the trucks never take a smoke break and never complain, and that's the whole sales pitch.
S0.fieldNote: Even in the calmest picture Zane's worry stays put, because the automation he fears is robotic haulage that already exists down the road. His union instincts kick in immediately. There's a small gap with his partner, who sees his fear as old news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need a union with teeth. If they're bringing in automation over a few years, then every driver gets retrained on full pay and nobody gets pushed out the gate. I'd say that at every meeting until people are sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the trucks come here within three years and I'm one of the drivers they don't keep for the control room. I'm good at driving, maybe the best on my crew at reading a wet ramp, but I'm no good with screens. And we're contractors, so we go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union hall the same week and get the contract drivers into the bargaining unit properly, because right now we're half in and half out. I'd stop the extra phone plan and the kids' swimming, maybe forty a week. And I'd go see the mayor with the others, because this town is one mine and one supermarket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like standing at the edge of the pit and feeling the ground give a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're no good with screens. If they offered you the control-room course, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably go, because Ngozi would make me. But I'd be the one asking the trainer to repeat everything while the young guys are already done. I never even use the AI thing on my phone, my daughter set it up and I deleted it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas, he's fifty-eight, he can't read well and he's the safest driver I've got. Nobody's going to retrain Tomas for a screen job. He'll be out, and he's got nowhere to go in this town.

S1.say: I'd tell everyone this is why miners need a strong union, with retraining on full pay and nobody pushed out. I'd keep saying it at every meeting until people were tired of hearing it.
S1.think: I really think driverless trucks reach our pit within three years and that contract drivers like me go first. I'm good at the wheel but weak with screens, so I doubt I'd be kept for the control room.
S1.do: Goes to the union hall that week to bring contract drivers fully into the bargaining unit. Cuts the extra phone plan and the kids' swimming to save about forty a week, and joins a group visit to the mayor.
S1.feel: Sick and unsteady, like the ground starting to give at the edge of the pit.
S1.quote: Nobody's going to retrain Tomas for a screen job.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change is already a direct threat to Zane because his job is the one robots are best at. He would only take retraining because his partner pushes him, which shows how strongly he resists new tools. His first instinct is collective, not personal: union, mayor, older crew members.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a crime being done to working people, and the government had better step in before the company fires everyone by text message. I'd want a law that says a company that replaces a worker with a machine pays into a fund for that worker. I'd put that on a sign and stand outside the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm finished in about a year. Two years is nothing, the trucks are already built, they just need the software to get cheap. With less than a month saved and a mortgage, we'd lose the house, that's the truth of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call a strike vote straight away, because the only power we have is before the trucks arrive. I'd ring the bank about freezing the mortgage before we miss a payment, not after. And I'd ask my brother in the city whether there's anything going, even though I don't want to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's already gone. I can't think past the bank letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd call a strike. What if the company says, fine, we'll bring the robots in sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then at least we went down standing up. But you're right, that's what they'd say, and half the crew would vote no because they're scared too. I don't have an answer for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son's twelve, he'd already know, he'd have seen it online. I'd tell him it's not his dad's fault and it's not the robot's fault either, it's the people who own them. I don't know if that helps a twelve-year-old.

S2.say: I'd call it a crime against working people and demand the government step in now. I'd want a law making companies that replace workers with machines pay into a fund for those workers.
S2.think: I think I'd be out within about a year, because the robot trucks already exist. With under a month saved and a mortgage, I believe we'd lose the house.
S2.do: Calls a strike vote straight away and phones the bank about freezing the mortgage before a payment is missed. Asks his brother in the city about work, though he doesn't want to leave town.
S2.feel: Overwhelmed, as if the ground has already gone, unable to think past the bank letter.
S2.quote: I'd tell him it's not his dad's fault and it's not the robot's fault either, it's the people who own them.
S2.fieldNote: Two years leaves Zane with no plan he believes in. When asked about the risk of a strike he admits he has no answer, which was a rare moment of doubt. His blame lands firmly on owners, not the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before but with more time to organise. I'd say we have five years to win the rules, so let's not waste the first three arguing. A tax on robot labour, a jobs guarantee for mining towns, that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years helps the union more than it helps me. I'd still be driving for maybe three of those years, which is three more years of mortgage paid, but I don't think I'd be any more ready for something else at the end. I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto the regional union council so I'm in the room, not just at the meetings. I'd try to pay an extra hundred a month off the mortgage while there's still a wage, which means no holiday and an old car. And maybe I'd look at the heavy-vehicle mechanic course at the college, though I'd put it off, I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more like a long night shift than a crash. You know it's coming, you just keep driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put the course off. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every time I sit in a classroom I'm fifteen again and failing maths. Driving I'm good at, in a classroom I'm nobody. Ngozi says that's pride, and she's not wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different at home in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop pretending we'll get ahead. Ngozi would probably take more shifts, which I hate, because she's already wrecked. And we'd tell the kids early, so the twelve-year-old isn't planning on the mine like I did.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years to win the rules and shouldn't waste three of them arguing. I'd push for a tax on robot labour and a jobs guarantee for mining towns.
S3.think: I think five years helps the union more than it helps me personally. I'd get a few more years of mortgage paid, but I doubt I'd be any readier for other work at the end.
S3.do: Joins the regional union council and tries to pay an extra hundred a month off the mortgage by skipping holidays. Considers the heavy-vehicle mechanic course at the college, but admits he would keep putting it off.
S3.feel: Anxious in a slow, grinding way, like a long night shift he has to keep driving through.
S3.quote: Every time I sit in a classroom I'm fifteen again and failing maths. Driving I'm good at, in a classroom I'm nobody.
S3.fieldNote: The extra years lower Zane's panic but don't change his core problem: he won't retrain and he knows it. He names his own pride as the obstacle, which felt honest. He also plans to steer his son away from mining early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse. If the company and the government let mining towns die with a decade's warning, that's a choice, and I'd say so loudly. I'd want the transition plan in writing, with names on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm fifty-three when it lands. That's too young to retire and too old for anyone to hire. The kids would be through school, which is the part that lets me breathe a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to win a retraining fund paid by the company, starting now, not in year nine. I'd probably do the mechanic course eventually, slowly, at night. And we'd try to get the mortgage down so it's nearly done by then, even if it means no new car for ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but it's a worry with a shape to it. I could plan around it, sort of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd keep putting the course off. Does ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me more time to put it off, to be honest. But maybe if two or three of the crew went together, I'd go. I'm better in a gang than on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would fifty-three-year-old Zane be doing, if it went well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fixing the robot trucks, maybe, if the union got us that deal. Or teaching young ones how to read a ramp before the trucks had a bad week. I can't really picture it, which tells you something.

S4.say: I'd say a decade's warning leaves no excuse, and letting mining towns die would be a choice. I'd want a written transition plan from the company and government, with names attached.
S4.think: I think ten years puts me at fifty-three when it lands, too young to retire and too old to be hired. The kids would be through school, and that's what lets me breathe a little.
S4.do: Pushes the union for a company-paid retraining fund starting now. Plans to take the mechanic course slowly at night, ideally with crew mates, and to pay the mortgage down by skipping a new car for ten years.
S4.feel: Still worried, but it is a worry with a shape he can plan around.
S4.quote: That's too young to retire and too old for anyone to hire.
S4.fieldNote: Zane's distress eases only a little with ten years, because his thin savings and resistance to retraining remain. The one opening was that he might study if crew mates went with him. He struggled to picture a good future, and he said so himself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. We'd be out of the house before I'd even worked out what happened. What would help is the company paying for the change it's making: full pay while we retrain, and a deal with the bank so miners in a robot transition can freeze the mortgage without wrecking their credit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's going to buy the copper. Everyone talks about robots doing the work, but the robots are digging for somebody. I'd like to know who gets the money when there's no drivers left to pay.

headlineQuote: I'd like to know who gets the money when there's no drivers left to pay.
portrait: Zane Okafor is a 43-year-old haul truck crew lead at a copper pit, a contract driver paid less than company staff, with a partner in home care, two kids and almost nothing saved. He already fears driverless trucks, which run at a sister mine, so even the AI Plateau picture leaves him uneasy. In the faster scenarios he reaches first for the union, the mayor and the law, and blames the owners rather than the machines. He admits he avoids retraining out of pride and fear of the classroom, and more warning time only softens, not removes, his alarm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he thinks the family would lose the house before he understood what had happened.
whatWouldHelp: Full pay from the company while workers retrain, and a bank deal letting miners in a robot transition freeze their mortgage without damaging their credit.
